title: Dave Roberts Addresses Josue De Paula's Spot on Dodgers Postseason Roster
author: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are under the biggest microscope in baseball as the regular season comes to a close. With October right around the corner, all eyes are on LA to see if they will win three consecutive championships for the first time in MLB in a quarter-century.
Superstar Shohei Ohtani has not been fully healthy essentially since the All-Star break, when he was scratched from not only his final start of the first half, but from all All-Star-related activities. After being shut down from pitching in early July, the concern has only grown coming out of an August where he only attained a .241 batting average for the month.
After Ohtani was placed on the injured list, Josue De Paula appeared to be the answer for the lack of Ohtani in the lineup.
Though it is obvious that De Paula will not be pitching, his offense has the potential to start to fill the enormous Ohtani-sized shoes. In Double-A, the 21-year-old slashed .303/.401/.547 with 27 home runs and 104 RBIs, leading to a call-up that preceded any Triple-A action.
De Paula was hitless during the first two games of his MLB career, but earned his first hit via a towering fourth-inning home run last Sunday.
Due to his astounding minor league track record, his 92.6 mph exit velocity at the MLB level thus far, and the fact that the organization didn't feel the need for him to move up to Triple-A, there have been murmurs as to what his spot on a postseason roster may be.
Manager Dave Roberts spoke on if De Paula should be under consideration for a roster spot, even though he will have less than a month of MLB knowledge come October.
“Yeah, he should be [under consideration],” Roberts said. “This is more of a trial run, no promises. Just obviously having Shohei down and giving a guy that’s performed well an opportunity. Then you just sort of see where it takes us.
"I think right now that’s kind of where we’re at and take it day to day. I just hope he continues to perform and take those at-bats and then we’ll kind of see where we’re at in September.”
Roberts also clarified that the rookie's status for the postseason even being a potential storyline says more about the maturity and talent of De Paula.
“It’s been good that you can even bring that question up,” Roberts said. “But it’s still very early as far as however many at-bats or plate appearances he has taken. But in this small sample, yeah, it’s been good. But it’s certainly a much different level of focus with the postseason. But baseball is still baseball. I hope he makes our decision hard.”
Across seven games thus far, De Paula is 3-for-18 (.167) with one home run, four RBIs, seven walks and an OPS of .789.

Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

title: Why Dodgers' top rookie of 2026 is not Josue De Paula
author: Conor Liguori
body:
Why Dodgers' top rookie of 2026 is not Josue De Paula originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers have no shortage of talent.
Even with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, the NL West club has one of, if not the best, rosters in the Majors.
Concerns about the bullpen are warranted. But a starting three in the rotation of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, and one of Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Justin Wrobleski is dominant.
With Ohtani on the IL, the Dodgers promoted a new talented prospect to replace him at designated hitter: slugger Josue De Paula.
De Paula promptly hit a homer just a few games into his first taste of the Majors and has a .789 OPS through 25 plate appearances.
But Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller believes it's too soon to label him the best Dodgers rookie of the season. Instead, Miller awarded that distinction to a middle infielder.
"There's already a case to be made for Josue De Paula in this spot, even though he just made his MLB debut as Shohei Ohtani's fill-in last Friday," Miller wrote.
"However, [Alex] Freeland spent much of the season as the Dodgers' primary second baseman, providing decent value with his glove while hitting just well enough to earn regular playing time."
Freeland doesn't have eye-popping offensive numbers, hitting .230 with four home runs and a 79 OPS+.
But he has +3 outs above average while playing at three infield spots, mainly second base.
De Paula could change Miller's mind during the final week of the regular season. Manager Dave Roberts should give him plenty of playing time.
For now, Freeland has done enough to warrant the title as the Dodgers' best rookie of the year.

title: Dodgers convierten el Oeste en su territorio y celebran otro título de división
author: Luis Del Valle
body:
Hay celebraciones que podrían convertirse en rutina, pero Los Angeles Dodgers se niegan a tratarlas como algo normal. La franquicia volvió a apoderarse del título de la División Oeste de la Liga Nacional al derrotar 8-2 a los Cincinnati Reds en el Great American Ball Park. Fue su quinto campeonato divisional consecutivo y el número 13 en las últimas 14 temporadas, otra cifra que dimensiona el dominio de Los Ángeles en esta etapa.
King Tuck! pic.twitter.com/FGbgOZjXXS
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 17, 2026
Kyle Tucker prendió la fiesta
La ofensiva encontró en Kyle Tucker a su principal protagonista. El jardinero terminó de 4 hits en 5 turnos, conectó un jonrón y produjo tres carreras, quedándose a un triple de completar el ciclo.
i love kyle tucker pic.twitter.com/ePeIAxm7re
— 🌱 jaime (@dodgersrpf) September 17, 2026
Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Josue De Paula y Miguel Rojas también impulsaron carreras para unos Dodgers que no necesitaron de un abridor tradicional. Justin Wrobleski trabajó tres entradas perfectas para iniciar un partido manejado desde el bullpen.
El triunfo dejó a Los Ángeles con marca de 93-60, nueve juegos por encima de los Padres de San Diego, que también ganaron durante la jornada pero ya no tenían forma matemática de alcanzar el liderato divisional.
Un dominio que parece no terminar
La dimensión del logro va mucho más allá de 2026.
Los Dodgers han conquistado el Oeste 13 veces durante sus últimas 14 campañas. La única excepción ocurrió en 2021, cuando los San Francisco Giants terminaron por delante de ellos.
Además, desde que MLB instauró el sistema divisional en 1969, Los Ángeles encabeza las Grandes Ligas con 24 campeonatos de división.
La franquicia también alcanzó su decimocuarta clasificación consecutiva a la postemporada, igualando la histórica racha de Atlanta entre 1991 y 2005.
Sights and sounds from the clubhouse. 👀 pic.twitter.com/0UTzHdvvpK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 18, 2026
Muncy todavía disfruta el champán
Pese a estar acostumbrado a estas celebraciones, Max Muncy dejó claro que el momento conserva su valor.
“Nunca lo doy por sentado”, aseguró el veterano durante la celebración, destacando lo especial que resulta poder festejar después de atravesar una temporada de 162 partidos.
Y esta vez hubo razones de sobra para descorchar las botellas. Los Dodgers ya habían asegurado días antes su presencia en octubre, pero conquistar la división les permitió completar otro de los grandes objetivos de la temporada regular.
Ahora viene lo que realmente quieren
El título del Oeste, sin embargo, no representa la meta definitiva.
Los Dodgers llegan a octubre como campeones consecutivos de las Series Mundiales de 2024 y 2025 y persiguen algo que ningún equipo consigue desde los Yankees de Nueva York de 1998, 1999 y 2000: levantar tres Clásicos de Otoño consecutivos.
La corona divisional confirma que la maquinaria sigue funcionando. Ahora el reto será convertir nuevamente ese dominio de seis meses en victorias durante octubre.

Fue su quinto campeonato divisional consecutivo y el número 13 en las últimas 14 temporadas, otra cifra que dimensiona el dominio de Los Ángeles en esta etapa.
King Tuck! pic.twitter.com/FGbgOZjXXS
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 17, 2026
Kyle Tucker prendió la fiesta
La ofensiva encontró en Kyle Tucker a su principal protagonista. El jardinero terminó de 4 hits en 5 turnos, conectó un jonrón y produjo tres carreras, quedándose a un triple de completar el ciclo.
i love kyle tucker pic.twitter.com/ePeIAxm7re
— 🌱 jaime (@dodgersrpf) September 17, 2026
Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Josue De Paula y Miguel Rojas también impulsaron carreras para unos Dodgers que no necesitaron de un abridor tradicional. Justin Wrobleski trabajó tres entradas perfectas para iniciar un partido manejado desde el bullpen.
El triunfo dejó a Los Ángeles con marca de 93-60, nueve juegos por encima de los Padres de San Diego, que también ganaron durante la jornada pero ya no tenían forma matemática de alcanzar el liderato divisional.
Un dominio que parece no terminar
La dimensión del logro va mucho más allá de 2026.
Los Dodgers han conquistado el Oeste 13 veces durante sus últimas 14 campañas. La única excepción ocurrió en 2021, cuando los San Francisco Giants terminaron por delante de ellos.
Además, desde que MLB instauró el sistema divisional en 1969, Los Ángeles encabeza las Grandes Ligas con 24 campeonatos de división.
La franquicia también alcanzó su decimocuarta clasificación consecutiva a la postemporada, igualando la histórica racha de Atlanta entre 1991 y 2005.
Sights and sounds from the clubhouse. 👀 pic.twitter.com/0UTzHdvvpK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 18, 2026
Muncy todavía disfruta el champán
Pese a estar acostumbrado a estas celebraciones, Max Muncy dejó claro que el momento conserva su valor.
“Nunca lo doy por sentado”, aseguró el veterano durante la celebración, destacando lo especial que resulta poder festejar después de atravesar una temporada de 162 partidos.
Y esta vez hubo razones de sobra para descorchar las botellas. Los Dodgers ya habían asegurado días antes su presencia en octubre, pero conquistar la división les permitió completar otro de los grandes objetivos de la temporada regular.
Ahora viene lo que realmente quieren
El título del Oeste, sin embargo, no representa la meta definitiva.
Los Dodgers llegan a octubre como campeones consecutivos de las Series Mundiales de 2024 y 2025 y persiguen algo que ningún equipo consigue desde los Yankees de Nueva York de 1998, 1999 y 2000: levantar tres Clásicos de Otoño consecutivos.
La corona divisional confirma que la maquinaria sigue funcionando. Ahora el reto será convertir nuevamente ese dominio de seis meses en victorias durante octubre.

title: Dodgers manager comments on future interest in Elly De La Cruz
author: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra
body:
Elly De La Cruz is enjoying a career year in his fourth season with the Cincinnati Reds, and it included plenty of success against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
That was an extension of De La Cruz’s career performance against the Dodgers, in which he’s hit .290 with seven home runs, 14 RBI and 17 runs scored in 26 career games.
“He’s definitely had a lot of success against us,” manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA when asked if felt as though De La Cruz was auditioning to become a Dodgers target.
“I still recall that homer he hit off (Noah) Syndergaard here. I know him enough through All-Star Games and things like that, that he likes the big stage, he wants to play against the best and against us, he certainly performs. I think there’s a lot of willing takers for that person and talent.
“It’s nice to win games against those guys and still kind of be a fan and marvel at what he can do on a baseball field. He’s very impressive.”
In seven games against the Dodgers this season, De La Cruz batted .360/.407/1.040 with two doubles, five home runs and nine RBI.
De La Cruz’s talent should make him a foundational building block who is untouchable in trade talks, but the Reds do not have a great track record of success over the past 12 seasons. Their only two playoff appearances since 2014 were the 16-team playoff in 2020 and as the last National League Wild Card team in 2025 with an 83-79 record.
Cincinnati has yet to lock him De La Cruz long term, but that could change with his performance this year elevating him to the upper echelon of MLB’s hierarchy. For now, he has three years of arbitration remaining before becoming a free agent in 2030 as a soon-to-be 28-year-old.
Mookie Betts’ contract doesn’t expire until after the 2032 season, but that would not prevent the Dodgers from making a play for De La Cruz. Nor would the investment they made in 2024 by drafting Kellon Lindsey with their first pitck.
Elly De La Cruz previously impressed Dave Roberts
De La Cruz made MLB debut against the Dodgers back in 2023, going 1-for-2 with a double. Roberts had high praise for the blossoming star that season.
“He is as toolsy as any player in the big leagues,” Roberts said prior to that weekend series beginning. “The way he carried himself, the poise on the field, on a Major League field, so early in his career was remarkable. He’s a human highlight film. I like watching the highlights much more than in real-time, firsthand.
“But what a special talent. It’s good for the game of baseball.”

title: Dodgers begin final homestand of the regular season hosting the Giants
author: Estevão Maximo
body:
The NL West crown has been secured, but the regular season grind carries on, with the next checkmark being a playoff bye, and if the Brewers stumble, maybe even the NL’s top record: the Dodgers open a series against the Giants, with the former looking like a near formality, four up on Atlanta with nine to go and threatening a Brewers team that’s only two games ahead after losing to the Pirates yesterday.
Dodgers begin final homestand of the regular season hosting the Giants
The Dodgers open a weekend set against a division rival they’ll face in six of their last nine games, the Giants
One might argue that more than specific and still important team accomplishments that the Dodgers may have between now and the end of the regular season, the key is to see individual players nearing their best form. For the purposes of this Friday game against the Giants, we’ll focus on Kyle Tucker and Tyler Glasnow, who fit the bill to a T of what we’re trying to discuss here.
Through his last eight games, Tucker isn’t just showing signs of life; he has been this team’s best hitter, securing 12 hits in just 29 at-bats and leaving the yard four times: the most home runs he has hit in such a short sample in the entire season. Outstanding during the road trip, Tucker has a chance to carry some momentum into the playoffs. At the same time, it’d be quite flat to see him reverse back into the hitter we’ve seen from most of the year as the team returns to Dodger Stadium, a place in which he carries a .572 OPS in 2026.
On the mound, it’ll be Tyler Glasnow, who, after returning from the IL with pristine control, walking just one batter in the first two starts back, has now walked seven in the last two, allowing a combined eight runs. Glasnow will be matched up against the offense with the lowest walk rate in baseball, the Giants at 7.5% BB%.
Tucker and Glasnow would be treated as the star players on most teams, but playing for the Dodgers, they serve slightly different roles even if the expectation for outstanding production is one and the same. Can Glasnow overcome his recent struggles while Tucker carries on in improved form? Standing in their way is the San Francisco Giants, a last-place club in everything but name, sitting in fourth place in the West with the second-worst record in the National League.
Friday game info
- Teams: Dodgers vs. Giants
- Ballpark: Dodger Stadium
- Start time: 7:15 p.m.
- TV: Apple TV
- Radio: AM 570 (English), KTNQ 1020 AM (Spanish)

title: Kyle Tucker’s flirtation with history gives Dodgers more hope of turnaround
author: Jack Harris
body:
Welcome to the California Post's weekly Dodgers recap, where we review the week that was, hand out very official awards and take stock of the state of the season.
PLAYER OF THE WEEK
Kyle Tucker (12-for-29 since Sept. 9; triple shy of the cycle on Thursday)
Off the bat, it appeared history was afoot.
Already on Thursday afternoon, Kyle Tucker had kicked his slow late-season turnaround into a suddenly more hopeful gear, hitting a two-run home run in the first, an RBI double in the second and a single that aided a three-run rally in the fourth.
Now, standing at the plate just a triple shy of the cycle in the eighth, he laced a line drive that made the feat feel possible.
With yet another squared-up swing, the $240 million slugger shot a ball into the left-center field gap. As two Reds outfielders converged on it, the entire Dodgers dugout rose in anticipation.
Alas, the 11th cycle in Dodgers history would have to wait.
The Reds turned a clean relay play. Tucker wisely — although, somewhat disappointingly, given the lopsided score — pulled up at second. And on the bench, all his teammates could do was razz him by mimicking send signs with their arms helplessly waving.
"I tried my best, but I don't think I was gonna get there," he told SportsNet LA afterward. "I probably would've been thrown out halfway."
Oh, well.
For this year's Dodgers, Tucker's 4-for-5, three-RBI game was still hugely encouraging, continuing what is now a weeklong surge in which the four-time All-Star has finally looked like himself.
Even before this stretch, the Dodgers committed to keeping Tucker as a key part of their lineup.
They hoped a breakthrough he made with his mechanics could salvage something from an otherwise disastrous debut campaign with the team.
Well, in his last eight games, Tucker has batted .414 with seven extra-base knocks, 10 RBIs and more walks (five) than strikeouts (four).
He has hit five home runs in his last 13 games, after collecting just 11 in his first 132 games this year.
It is the version of Tucker that the Dodgers will need in the playoffs, especially with fellow left-handed bats like Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman battling ongoing injuries.
After a season that once seemed so lost, signs of revival have arrived just in time.
PITCHERS OF THE WEEK
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto (seven scoreless innings from each)
We are going with a tandem honor this week, from a pair of pitchers who will likely have the biggest influence on the Dodgers' World Series chances.
With Blake Snell battling a groin injury, and Tyler Glasnow entering a Friday start having recently regressed in his return from the injured list, the Dodgers' rotation doesn't feel quite as formidable as it once did.
Then again, if Skubal and Yamamoto keep pitching like they did this week — when they spun consecutive scoreless seven-inning outings in Cincinnati — those other question marks might not feel so daunting.
Both pitchers have sterling postseason track records: Yamamoto with a 7-1 record and 2.25 ERA in 10 playoff outings (including last year's World Series heroics) and Skubal with a 2-1 record and 2.04 ERA in six October appearances of his own (all with the Tigers the last two years).
Either could anchor a pitching staff on their own capable of making a run to the Fall Classic.
Together, they give the Dodgers arguably the best 1-2 punch in the majors. This week, they delivered the club's first pair of back-to-back scoreless seven-inning outings since 2022 when Tyler Anderson and Clayton Kershaw did it.
Granted, dominating the Reds in mid-September is not the same as producing gems in the playoffs.
But with so many other concerns mounting at the moment, Skubal and Yamamoto at least represent a pillar of potential pitching excellence to lean on, one that could compensate for other shortcomings in the Dodgers' three-peat bid.
PROSPECT OF THE WEEK
The entire Dodgers' minor-league system
The Dodgers' big-league club hasn't been the only one popping bottles in beer-soaked clubhouse celebrations recently.
This year, all four of the organization's minor-league affiliates also clinched places in their respective playoffs, with Triple-A Oklahoma City completing the quad-fecta by winning the second-half title in the Pacific Coast League on Wednesday.
It marks the first time the Dodgers have had four affiliates make the playoffs since 2019 (and that year included their now-defunct rookie-ball outpost in Ogden, Utah).
It's also the latest reminder about the strength of depth they boast in their highly touted farm system.
"I know people don't care about minor-league win percentages, but we kind of do," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes told the California Post earlier this season. "I think it's a good proxy of how well your farm system is performing and how to understand what it takes to win."
Three of the club's affiliates have already been eliminated, with Double-A Tulsa, High-A Great Lakes and Single-A Ontario all losing in their division championship series.
OKC, meanwhile, will begin its postseason push next week in the best-of-three PCL Championship Series against the Athletics' Las Vegas affiliate. If they win that, they will remain in Vegas for the Triple-A National Championship Game against the winner of the International League.
QUESTION OF THE WEEK
Who should Dodgers hope to see in the first round of the playoffs?
With the NL West crown secured, the Dodgers still have work to do over the season's final nine games.
Given their injury problems, they've never needed a first-round bye so badly.
The good news: They remain four games up on the Braves for the NL's No. 2 seed, with their magic number down to six for securing passage straight to the NL Division Series.
And though they remain two games back of the Brewers for the best record in the majors — and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs — conventional wisdom in recent weeks has suggested that the playoff through the postseason might be better from the 2-seed anyway.
Now, however, the NL playoff field is getting muddied, with the red-hot Padres sitting just one game back of the Cubs and Phillies.
So, who should Dodgers fans root to see in a potential first-round matchup? Well, it depends on what kind of matchup you think suits the Dodgers best.
The Cubs and Phillies had seemed like tougher draws than the Braves or Padres, thanks to Chicago's deep and homer-happy lineup and the Phillies' powerhouse starting rotation trio.
But this week, Philadelphia lost one of its star pitchers, Jesús Luzardo, to a shoulder injury that has put his playoff availability in doubt. The Cubs, meanwhile, have seen their offense cool off and still face questions with an unimposing starting rotation.
The Braves have their own flaws (they've been a middle-of-the-pack offense since the All-Star break) but still boast Chris Sale at the top of their rotation.
The Padres, on the other hand, are making a familiar late-season surge and have a habit of playing the Dodgers tough in the playoffs.
It will all make for a fascinating final few days of scoreboard watching, with a slew of new postseason permutations now on the table.
The Dodgers, of course, won't be overly worried about who they might square off against. Their focus is on continuing to play a better brand of all-around baseball — and making sure they avoid the best-of-three wild-card round.

Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto (seven scoreless innings from each)
We are going with a tandem honor this week, from a pair of pitchers who will likely have the biggest influence on the Dodgers' World Series chances.
With Blake Snell battling a groin injury, and Tyler Glasnow entering a Friday start having recently regressed in his return from the injured list, the Dodgers' rotation doesn't feel quite as formidable as it once did.
Then again, if Skubal and Yamamoto keep pitching like they did this week — when they spun consecutive scoreless seven-inning outings in Cincinnati — those other question marks might not feel so daunting.
Both pitchers have sterling postseason track records: Yamamoto with a 7-1 record and 2.25 ERA in 10 playoff outings (including last year's World Series heroics) and Skubal with a 2-1 record and 2.04 ERA in six October appearances of his own (all with the Tigers the last two years).
Either could anchor a pitching staff on their own capable of making a run to the Fall Classic.
Together, they give the Dodgers arguably the best 1-2 punch in the majors. This week, they delivered the club's first pair of back-to-back scoreless seven-inning outings since 2022 when Tyler Anderson and Clayton Kershaw did it.
Granted, dominating the Reds in mid-September is not the same as producing gems in the playoffs.
But with so many other concerns mounting at the moment, Skubal and Yamamoto at least represent a pillar of potential pitching excellence to lean on, one that could compensate for other shortcomings in the Dodgers' three-peat bid.
PROSPECT OF THE WEEK
The entire Dodgers' minor-league system
The Dodgers' big-league club hasn't been the only one popping bottles in beer-soaked clubhouse celebrations recently.
This year, all four of the organization's minor-league affiliates also clinched places in their respective playoffs, with Triple-A Oklahoma City completing the quad-fecta by winning the second-half title in the Pacific Coast League on Wednesday.
It marks the first time the Dodgers have had four affiliates make the playoffs since 2019 (and that year included their now-defunct rookie-ball outpost in Ogden, Utah).
It's also the latest reminder about the strength of depth they boast in their highly touted farm system.
"I know people don't care about minor-league win percentages, but we kind of do," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes told the California Post earlier this season. "I think it's a good proxy of how well your farm system is performing and how to understand what it takes to win."
Three of the club's affiliates have already been eliminated, with Double-A Tulsa, High-A Great Lakes and Single-A Ontario all losing in their division championship series.
OKC, meanwhile, will begin its postseason push next week in the best-of-three PCL Championship Series against the Athletics' Las Vegas affiliate. If they win that, they will remain in Vegas for the Triple-A National Championship Game against the winner of the International League.
QUESTION OF THE WEEK
Who should Dodgers hope to see in the first round of the playoffs?
With the NL West crown secured, the Dodgers still have work to do over the season's final nine games.
Given their injury problems, they've never needed a first-round bye so badly.
The good news: They remain four games up on the Braves for the NL's No. 2 seed, with their magic number down to six for securing passage straight to the NL Division Series.
And though they remain two games back of the Brewers for the best record in the majors — and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs — conventional wisdom in recent weeks has suggested that the playoff through the postseason might be better from the 2-seed anyway.
Now, however, the NL playoff field is getting muddied, with the red-hot Padres sitting just one game back of the Cubs and Phillies.
So, who should Dodgers fans root to see in a potential first-round matchup? Well, it depends on what kind of matchup you think suits the Dodgers best.
The Cubs and Phillies had seemed like tougher draws than the Braves or Padres, thanks to Chicago's deep and homer-happy lineup and the Phillies' powerhouse starting rotation trio.
But this week, Philadelphia lost one of its star pitchers, Jesús Luzardo, to a shoulder injury that has put his playoff availability in doubt. The Cubs, meanwhile, have seen their offense cool off and still face questions with an unimposing starting rotation.
The Braves have their own flaws (they've been a middle-of-the-pack offense since the All-Star break) but still boast Chris Sale at the top of their rotation.
The Padres, on the other hand, are making a familiar late-season surge and have a habit of playing the Dodgers tough in the playoffs.
It will all make for a fascinating final few days of scoreboard watching, with a slew of new postseason permutations now on the table.
The Dodgers, of course, won't be overly worried about who they might square off against. Their focus is on continuing to play a better brand of all-around baseball — and making sure they avoid the best-of-three wild-card round.
rss_title: Kyle Tucker’s flirtation with history gives Dodgers more hope of turnaround
rss_body:
Welcome to the California Post's weekly Dodgers recap, where we review the week that was, hand out very official awards and take stock of the state of the season.
PLAYER OF THE WEEK
Kyle Tucker (12-for-29 since Sept. 9; triple shy of the cycle on Thursday)

Now, standing at the plate just a triple shy of the cycle in the eighth, he laced a line drive that made the feat feel possible.
With yet another squared-up swing, the $240 million slugger shot a ball into the left-center field gap. As two Reds outfielders converged on it, the entire Dodgers dugout rose in anticipation.
Alas, the 11th cycle in Dodgers history would have to wait.
The Reds turned a clean relay play. Tucker wisely — although, somewhat disappointingly, given the lopsided score — pulled up at second. And on the bench, all his teammates could do was razz him by mimicking send signs with their arms helplessly waving.
"I tried my best, but I don't think I was gonna get there," he told SportsNet LA afterward. "I probably would've been thrown out halfway."
Oh, well.
For this year's Dodgers, Tucker's 4-for-5, three-RBI game was still hugely encouraging, continuing what is now a weeklong surge in which the four-time All-Star has finally looked like himself.
Even before this stretch, the Dodgers committed to keeping Tucker as a key part of their lineup.
They hoped a breakthrough he made with his mechanics could salvage something from an otherwise disastrous debut campaign with the team.

He has hit five home runs in his last 13 games, after collecting just 11 in his first 132 games this year.

title: Move over, Lakers. Not so fast, Rams. Dodgers are NL West champions again — and still LA’s team
author: Dylan Hernandez
body:
The Dodgers are the National League West champions.
Again.
They have won their division 13 times in the last 14 seasons, and the one time in that period in which they didn’t, they won a then-club-record 106 games.
Somewhere along the way, the Dodgers did the impossible: They met the requirements to become the sports franchise Los Angeles demanded.
Appreciating what this means requires an understanding of how Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant transformed this city in the early 2000s,
With O’Neal and Bryant as their stars, the Lakers didn’t just win championships.
They were unbeatable.
This image was reinforced by the play of O’Neal, a 7-foot-1, 325-pound freak of nature who literally couldn’t be stopped.
By the time the Lakers completed their three-peat in 2002, championships were no longer something Los Angeles hoped for.
They became something the city expected.
This is the standard used to measure teams with aspirations of becoming a cultural touchstone in this congested market. With plenty of other entertainment options, casual fans won’t invest too much of their time and money in a team unless they believe it will create the kind of citywide pride O’Neal’s Lakers once did.
The Lakers haven’t been that team for some time. The Rams are producing a worthy on-field product, but they remain in the process of winning back fans they lost over the two decades they spent in St. Louis.
The Dodgers are the one team in town that is clearing the bar.
“What’s funny is Los Angeles has always been looked at, as far as sports, (as) a Laker town,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I think we might have the market share right now in Los Angeles. It’s great. I think we draw more fans than anyone in the world, obviously, with the home dates we have. But it’s 40,000, 50,000 every night. We travel well. I do think the guys see it. They feed off it.”
The Dodgers managed to do this despite playing a sport that is particularly hard to dominate. The Lakers could dump the ball into O’Neal 30 times a game. The Dodgers have employed a number of Hall of Famers over the years, but as great as Shohei Ohtani is, he can only hit four times a game, maybe five.
The Dodgers have become a different kind of juggernaut.
With substantial investment from their owners, they have built some of the deepest rosters in baseball history. In its first season operating the team, Guggenheim Baseball Management signed All-Star outfielder Andre Ethier to an $85 million extension, picked up a then-unknown Yasiel Puig for $42 million, traded for All-Star infielder Hanley Ramirez and assumed more than $260 million in contract obligations in a blockbuster trade for Adrian Gonzalez, Carl Crawford and Josh Beckett.
Season after season, the Dodgers fielded one of the most expensive teams in the major leagues — if not the most expensive team.
Which is why at some point in each of the last 14 seasons, the Dodgers were considered favorites to win the World Series.
They are well into their second decade as baseball’s model franchise — or, depending on the perspective, Evil Empire. The last time they didn’t reach the playoffs, the world was a completely different place. LeBron James had just won his first NBA championship. “Gangnam Style” was a global phenomenon. The recreational use of marijuana was still outlawed in every jurisdiction of the United States.
There’s an entire generation of fans who don’t know what it’s like for the Dodgers to not be legitimate contenders.
Consistency by itself didn’t turn the Dodgers into the Dodgers of today. Actually winning championships was important, of course, and doing that required them to adjust how they built their rosters.
President of baseball operations Andrew Friedman used to operate as if the playoffs were a crapshoot. The organization’s focus was on the regular season, on just reaching the postseason. Because depth is required to survive a 162-game schedule, quantity was emphasized over quality.
The approach didn’t produce any championships. The Dodgers reached the World Series twice in their first eight seasons under Guggenheim ownership but lost both times.
The failures prompted them to pursue real difference-makers.
Mookie Betts, who was the catalyst of the championship team in 2020. Freddie Freeman, the home run hero of the 2024 World Series. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, the Most Valuable Player of the 2025 World Series. And, of course, Ohtani, the franchise’s most transformative player since Fernando Valenzuela, or maybe even Jackie Robinson.
The Dodgers have won three of the last six World Series.
Even with Ohtani dealing with right arm and left knee injuries, they will open the postseason as the odds-on favorites to win their third consecutive championship.
As fragmented as Los Angeles can be, most of the city can get behind that.

title: With another NL West title in hand, the prospect of October without Shohei Ohtani looms large for the Dodgers
author: Jake Mintz
body:
CINCINNATI — As the celebrating Los Angeles Dodgers drenched one another in various carbonated boozes, the team's most important character was bone dry and most likely quite sober roughly two thousand miles away.
Shohei Ohtani, that baseballing mover of mountains, is injured. A laundry list of ailing body parts — biceps, knee, neck — first kept the two-way dynamo from pitching, then frayed his offensive impact and finally rendered him physically incapable of taking the field. Last week, the Dodgers placed him on the IL, with just a few weeks left for him to recover before the start of the postseason and only five games between his earliest eligible return date and the end of the regular season.
Publicly, the club has maintained an optimistic tone, describing his issues as manageable, not season-ending. A return before the end of the regular season is still in play, skipper Dave Roberts reaffirmed this week. Yet nobody around the game would be shocked if the Dodgers opt for caution and keep Ohtani sidelined until October. Los Angeles' worst-case scenario, of course, would be a postseason without its main man.
So when the Dodgers embarked on their recent two-city swing, their $700 million slugger stayed back in Southern California. He rested, received treatment and hit off a tee — or, as Roberts vaguely put it, "continued his progression."
"Overall, [his] body feels normal-ish," Roberts said before Thursday's clincher. "Then it's kind of getting his body, his knee, his arm, biceps, whatever, back to full strength."
This marked the first time in the Dodgers' Ohtani Era that the man himself did not accompany the team for the entirety of a road trip. In fact, the most recent occurrence of a Dodgers club flying home without Ohtani came in October 2023, after the team's sweep loss to the Diamondbacks in that year's NLDS. Lance Lynn, Austin Barnes and a decade of frustration were on board that plane. Ohtani was still technically an Angel. In other words, it's been a while.
With the two-way superstar now the center of the Dodgers' solar system — and, to a large extent, the league's extended universe — Ohtani's absence this week in Cincinnati was easy to sense, impossible to avoid. Throughout the week, all about the yard, were reminders both big and small.
The blue bat bags lined up outside the locker room in numerical order went right from Will Smith's No. 16 to Kyle Tucker's No. 23, with no No. 17 to be found. Dodgers head security guard Al Garcia, typically within eyesight of Ohtani at all times, floated around the clubhouse with an uncharacteristically laid-back comportment buoyed by his relatively light list of duties.
A group of passionate Dodgers fans recognized the star's absence with a homemade sign that read "Feel Better Shohei, Give Decoy A Hug," making reference to Ohtani's dog. Even Yoshinobu Yamamoto admitted that it was odd not having Ohtani around, delivering one of his funnier and more cutting lines of the season.
"It's been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse," Yamamoto said via interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. "Although I have Roki [Sasaki], he doesn't really talk to me."
The Dodgers' lineup missed Ohtani, too, averaging less than four runs per game on the road trip before Thursday's eight-run outburst against a bottom-five Cincinnati pitching staff. Utilityman Tommy Edman got the bulk of leadoff duties, with Mookie Betts and rookie call-up Josue De Paula getting a day each in the one-hole. Edman went just 1-for-23 on the trip. Freddie Freeman's power dip continued, with five singles and nothing else. Will Smith has yet to really pop off since his return from the IL on Sept. 1.
"It feels different because he's such a presence when he's on the field," Roberts admitted Monday.
Therein lies the lingering concern. The Dodgers and Ohtani have all but accepted that he won't pitch again this season. That's not the end of the world; Los Angeles has the arms to solve that problem. On the other hand, navigating October without Ohtani at full-go would be a difficult proposition.
Ohtani's health, too, is not binary. Even if he plays, which at this point feels likely, he's unlikely to be completely healed. That dynamic could very well hamper his performance. Ohtani, overly cautious as they come, revealed that concern the last time he spoke to reporters on Sept. 8.
"I should have enough experience to address any kinks or injuries or anything like that with the swing," Ohtani said. "I'm going to use this as an opportunity to add on to the experience that I've had previously and address it regardless."
It's not exactly the most reassuring explanation — Ohtani implying that he'll need to manage his various discomforts for the rest of the season. How that process transpires and how productive Ohtani proves to be in October could determine how many Champagne celebrations he'll get to participate in this year.

With the two-way superstar now the center of the Dodgers' solar system — and, to a large extent, the league's extended universe — Ohtani's absence this week in Cincinnati was easy to sense, impossible to avoid. Throughout the week, all about the yard, were reminders both big and small.
The blue bat bags lined up outside the locker room in numerical order went right from Will Smith's No. 16 to Kyle Tucker's No. 23, with no No. 17 to be found. Dodgers head security guard Al Garcia, typically within eyesight of Ohtani at all times, floated around the clubhouse with an uncharacteristically laid-back comportment buoyed by his relatively light list of duties.
A group of passionate Dodgers fans recognized the star's absence with a homemade sign that read "Feel Better Shohei, Give Decoy A Hug," making reference to Ohtani's dog. Even Yoshinobu Yamamoto admitted that it was odd not having Ohtani around, delivering one of his funnier and more cutting lines of the season.
"It's been a weird feeling because I talk to him all the time in the clubhouse," Yamamoto said via interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. "Although I have Roki [Sasaki], he doesn't really talk to me."
The Dodgers' lineup missed Ohtani, too, averaging less than four runs per game on the road trip before Thursday's eight-run outburst against a bottom-five Cincinnati pitching staff. Utilityman Tommy Edman got the bulk of leadoff duties, with Mookie Betts and rookie call-up Josue De Paula getting a day each in the one-hole. Edman went just 1-for-23 on the trip. Freddie Freeman's power dip continued, with five singles and nothing else. Will Smith has yet to really pop off since his return from the IL on Sept. 1.
"It feels different because he's such a presence when he's on the field," Roberts admitted Monday.
Therein lies the lingering concern. The Dodgers and Ohtani have all but accepted that he won't pitch again this season. That's not the end of the world; Los Angeles has the arms to solve that problem. On the other hand, navigating October without Ohtani at full-go would be a difficult proposition.
Ohtani's health, too, is not binary. Even if he plays, which at this point feels likely, he's unlikely to be completely healed. That dynamic could very well hamper his performance. Ohtani, overly cautious as they come, revealed that concern the last time he spoke to reporters on Sept. 8.
"I should have enough experience to address any kinks or injuries or anything like that with the swing," Ohtani said. "I'm going to use this as an opportunity to add on to the experience that I've had previously and address it regardless."
It's not exactly the most reassuring explanation — Ohtani implying that he'll need to manage his various discomforts for the rest of the season. How that process transpires and how productive Ohtani proves to be in October could determine how many Champagne celebrations he'll get to participate in this year.

Here are the odds, probable pitchers, and predictions for Giants vs. Dodgers on Friday, Sept. 18.
Giants vs. Dodgers Odds, Run Line and Total

- Dodgers -1.5 (-137)

Tyler Glasnow has allowed four runs in each of his last two starts, going six innings against the Nationals and four innings against the Marlins. He hhasad allowed four runs in 12 innings in his first two starts back from injury.

- How to Watch (TV): Apple TV

I wouldn’t be shocked if the Dodgers got most of these eight runs themselves, and the Giants are capable of putting a few on the board.

title: Alexander: Can the Dodgers overcome the curse of the big contracts?
author: Jim Alexander
body:
The world according to Jim:
• Would it drive fans in other cities even further out of their minds if the Dodgers wound up three-peating despite minimal contributions from their two big free-agent signings of last winter? …
• Kyle Tucker (four years, $240 million all told, $55 million in 2026 including a $54 million signing bonus according to Cot’s Contracts), might be starting to wake up at the plate after struggling to justify that contract for the first six-plus months. In the past eight games going into Friday night’s series opener against the Giants, he has a slash line of .310/.566/.586 with five homers, 11 RBIs and 14 runs scored in 29 at-bats.
Then again, that has come exclusively against the Cincinnati and Miami pitching staffs. But Tucker’s contract hasn’t been totally sunk money in this first year. …
• Edwin Díaz, on the other hand, signed for three years, $69 million total, and $23 million this season including a $9 million signing bonus. As of now, that comes to $3.285 million per save. In fairness, he got the win in two of his four blown saves – three of which came in August, two in back-to-back appearances in Arizona – but he has hardly been what the Dodgers envisioned when they signed him.
And he has been active 45 of a possible 178 days this season. He spent all of May, June and most of July on the injured list after a procedure to remove “loose bodies” from his elbow, and went back on the IL on Aug. 18 with neck inflammation. He’s set to be activated Friday, but barring some absolutely lights-out performances over the next two weeks, it’ll be a stretch to imagine him being on the Dodgers’ initial postseason roster. …
• I’d like to be snarky here and suggest that this proves big free-agent signings by themselves don’t automatically lead to championships – but the Mets have already proven that. …
• It became official this week and probably shouldn’t be a surprise: The Kings appointed Drew Doughty as captain, succeeding the retired Anze Kopitar. Given what Doughty has devoted to this franchise in 18 seasons and 1,279 games, including L.A.’s first Stanley Cups in 2012 and 2014, it’s appropriate.
And, yes, we’re already speculating who will ultimately succeed Doughty, who turns 37 in December. Adrian Kempe, Artemi Panarin and Mikey Anderson will be the assistant captains this season … and my money’s on Mikey to eventually inherit the C on his sweater. …
• This week’s quiz: Doughty will be the Kings’ 15th captain dating to the franchise’s inception in 1967. How many of the other 14 can you name? Answer below.
• The Kings, incidentally, begin their preseason Saturday night at Ontario’s Toyota Arena against Las Vegas. Their farm club, the Ontario Reign, will be wearing purple and gold along with black this coming season. (And in an apparent nod to original Kings owner Jack Kent Cooke, who loved the color purple but hated the word and thus decreed that it officially be called Forum Blue, the Reign will label theirs as Inland Blue.)
Can we convince the big club to add those colors, too? …
• Quiz answer: Bob Wall, Larry Cahan, Bob Pulford (one season before he was named head coach in 1972), Terry Harper, Mike Murphy, Dave Lewis, Terry Ruskowski, Dave Taylor, Wayne Gretzky, Luc Robitaille (as an interim captain early in the 1992-93 season while Gretzky was laid up with a back injury), Rob Blake (who succeeded Gretzky after the Great One was traded to St. Louis Feb. 27, 1996), Mattias Norstrom, Dustin Brown and Kopitar. …
• Meanwhile, across the county line, Ducks general manager Pat Verbeek got Cutter Gauthier’s signature on the dotted line of a six-year, $81 million deal just three hours before a more restrictive collective bargaining agreement took effect at 9 p.m. Pacific time Wednesday night.
You think Verbeek is like many of us were in school – and as, indeed, some of us still are? It takes a hard deadline to get anything done. …
• No need to rehash what happened last weekend, but this needs to be said: ESPN sideline reporter Holly Rowe handled herself with far more grace than those misogynist creeps who felt compelled to weigh in, as well as the idiot who generated the disgusting fake video of Steve Sarkisian slapping Rowe (and all of those who laughed about it). May that cretin have his AI toys taken away.
I’m with Team Holly. And this is yet another reminder of the garbage that women in sports media generally have to endure for no reason other than their gender. …
• UCLA’s new athletics CEO, Tim Harris, posted a large, blue W this week when he announced students now can attend football and men’s and women’s basketball games for free. This is how you (a) amp up the atmosphere at home games and (b) promote the loyalty that turns alumni into supporters and donors.
Next suggestion: Convince a corporate donor to sponsor those rooter buses from Westwood to the Rose Bowl and make them free as well. …
• The Pro Football Hall of Fame is cutting the size of its voting panel by almost half, from 50 to 28. Meanwhile, 428 ballots were cast in baseball’s Hall of Fame election last year by voting members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (and yes, I am one). Additionally, football Hall of Fame selectors are sworn to secrecy while BBWAA voters are encouraged to show their work, and most of us do.
Is it any wonder, then, that the general public seems far more invested in who gets to Cooperstown every year than in who gets selected for the shrine in Canton? …
• The Awful Announcing platform had this headline the other day: “Has sports on streaming failed?” The reaction (overreaction?) was to the opening week NFL ratings, with NBC’s New England-Seattle game Wednesday drawing far better national ratings than Netflix’s Rams-49ers game from Melbourne the following night.
Hidden in those numbers is a simple truth: A network over-the-air broadcast will always do better because it is more accessible – especially for those who can’t or won’t pay for all the streaming services that televise sports.
And maybe this is the pertinent question: Is the league working for the streaming service, and if so shouldn’t it be the other way around? At the very least, teams and leagues should insist that the streamer’s telecast be shown in the competing teams’ markets on either their regular TV outlets or, as the NFL does, an over-the-air channel.
jalexander@scng.com

• This week’s quiz: Doughty will be the Kings’ 15th captain dating to the franchise’s inception in 1967. How many of the other 14 can you name? Answer below.
• The Kings, incidentally, begin their preseason Saturday night at Ontario’s Toyota Arena against Las Vegas. Their farm club, the Ontario Reign, will be wearing purple and gold along with black this coming season. (And in an apparent nod to original Kings owner Jack Kent Cooke, who loved the color purple but hated the word and thus decreed that it officially be called Forum Blue, the Reign will label theirs as Inland Blue.)
Can we convince the big club to add those colors, too? …
• Quiz answer: Bob Wall, Larry Cahan, Bob Pulford (one season before he was named head coach in 1972), Terry Harper, Mike Murphy, Dave Lewis, Terry Ruskowski, Dave Taylor, Wayne Gretzky, Luc Robitaille (as an interim captain early in the 1992-93 season while Gretzky was laid up with a back injury), Rob Blake (who succeeded Gretzky after the Great One was traded to St. Louis Feb. 27, 1996), Mattias Norstrom, Dustin Brown and Kopitar. …
• Meanwhile, across the county line, Ducks general manager Pat Verbeek got Cutter Gauthier’s signature on the dotted line of a six-year, $81 million deal just three hours before a more restrictive collective bargaining agreement took effect at 9 p.m. Pacific time Wednesday night.
You think Verbeek is like many of us were in school – and as, indeed, some of us still are? It takes a hard deadline to get anything done. …
• No need to rehash what happened last weekend, but this needs to be said: ESPN sideline reporter Holly Rowe handled herself with far more grace than those misogynist creeps who felt compelled to weigh in, as well as the idiot who generated the disgusting fake video of Steve Sarkisian slapping Rowe (and all of those who laughed about it). May that cretin have his AI toys taken away.
I’m with Team Holly. And this is yet another reminder of the garbage that women in sports media generally have to endure for no reason other than their gender. …
• UCLA’s new athletics CEO, Tim Harris, posted a large, blue W this week when he announced students now can attend football and men’s and women’s basketball games for free. This is how you (a) amp up the atmosphere at home games and (b) promote the loyalty that turns alumni into supporters and donors.
Next suggestion: Convince a corporate donor to sponsor those rooter buses from Westwood to the Rose Bowl and make them free as well. …
• The Pro Football Hall of Fame is cutting the size of its voting panel by almost half, from 50 to 28. Meanwhile, 428 ballots were cast in baseball’s Hall of Fame election last year by voting members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (and yes, I am one). Additionally, football Hall of Fame selectors are sworn to secrecy while BBWAA voters are encouraged to show their work, and most of us do.
Is it any wonder, then, that the general public seems far more invested in who gets to Cooperstown every year than in who gets selected for the shrine in Canton? …
• The Awful Announcing platform had this headline the other day: “Has sports on streaming failed?” The reaction (overreaction?) was to the opening week NFL ratings, with NBC’s New England-Seattle game Wednesday drawing far better national ratings than Netflix’s Rams-49ers game from Melbourne the following night.
Hidden in those numbers is a simple truth: A network over-the-air broadcast will always do better because it is more accessible – especially for those who can’t or won’t pay for all the streaming services that televise sports.
And maybe this is the pertinent question: Is the league working for the streaming service, and if so shouldn’t it be the other way around? At the very least, teams and leagues should insist that the streamer’s telecast be shown in the competing teams’ markets on either their regular TV outlets or, as the NFL does, an over-the-air channel.

title: Dodgers manager Dave Roberts makes Edwin Diaz decision
author: Matt Larter
body:
The MLB postseason is approaching, and the Los Angeles Dodgers are preparing to welcome relief pitcher Edwin Diaz back from the injured list as they look to finalize their bullpen for another World Series run.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts has confirmed that Diaz will be activated Friday ahead of the team's three-game weekend series against the San Francisco Giants. However, the veteran reliever will not immediately return to the high-leverage role he was expected to occupy when he signed with Los Angeles.
Diaz will have to earn high-leverage opportunities
Mar 31, 2026; Los Angeles, California, USA; Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Edwin Diaz (3) throws against the Cleveland Guardians during the ninth inning at Dodger Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Gary A. Vasquez-Imagn Images
Roberts said Diaz will initially be used in lower-leverage situations when he returns and will have to "earn" his way into higher-leverage spots. The approach gives the Dodgers an opportunity to gradually reintegrate the right-hander while evaluating his performance and health ahead of the postseason.
Diaz has been sidelined since mid-August with a neck injury. His current absence is the latest setback in a difficult first season with the Dodgers after the club signed him to a three-year, $69 million contract with the expectation that he would serve as its closer.
The 32-year-old has also dealt with an elbow issue this season, undergoing arthroscopic surgery in April to remove loose bodies from his right elbow.
MORE: Wilson Contreras is 'frustrated' & calls out Red Sox
Dodgers face decision ahead of postseason
Diaz's numbers have made his return particularly intriguing. He has appeared in just 13.2 innings this season and owns an 11.85 ERA and 2.56 WHIP. He has allowed 18 runs on 25 hits during that limited workload.
With the postseason approaching, the Dodgers appear unlikely to immediately hand the closer role back to Diaz. Instead, Roberts' comments suggest the veteran will need to demonstrate that he can consistently get outs before being trusted in the most important moments of games.
Still, having Diaz available gives Los Angeles another experienced arm to evaluate as the playoffs draw closer. The Dodgers enter the final stretch of the regular season in a comfortable position, sitting nine games ahead of the San Diego Padres in the National League Central with nine games remaining.
Diaz is expected to be active for Friday's series opener against the Giants, giving him an opportunity to begin working his way back into the Dodgers' bullpen plans.

title: Tarik Skubal Shares Eyebrow Raising Comment After Los Angeles Dodgers Clinching Moment
author: TJ French
body:
In case you forgot or don’t know… the Los Angeles Dodgers won the NL West on Thursday afternoon, defeating the Reds 8-2.
LA celebrated in the Reds’ visiting clubhouse, giving the LA media access to all the players as they celebrated.
Reporters got a hold of ace starter Tarik Skubal, who shared an eyebrow-raising comment about the Los Angeles Dodgers’ future.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Quietly Announce 6 Roster Moves Before Astros Series
Tarik Skubal Gets Too Honest After Dodgers Clinching Moment
Per @SportsNetLA, here is a funny exchange between Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell:
Skubal: “It’s gonna be special. It’s gonna be the first of many.”
Snell: “Tell em it’s gonna be special because you’re playing this postseason with your boy.”
Skubal: “This is my best friend; he’s my little brother.”
What I want to focus on, and something that’s been noted in other reports, is Skubal using the phrase “it’s gonna be the first of many”.
Skubal, of course, is an impending free agent after the season, so is he saying this will be the first of many division crowns with LA?? Or just generally in his career?? Hmmmm….
More MLB on Heavy: Josue De Paula Makes Honest Dodgers Statement After NL West Clinch
Tarik Skubal Since Joining the Dodgers
There haven’t been any public talks about Tarik Skubal’s upcoming contract demands, but baseball pundits believe it could be in the range of $350-400 million when all said and done.
After being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers, Tarik Skubal has been spectacular, per usual.
He’s made eight starts since joining LA, and Skubal has an ERA of 2.52 in 50 innings during that span with 57 strikeouts and a WHIP of 1.040.
Adding Skubal makes the Dodgers a dominant threat in the MLB playoffs, and LA will surely be a tough out come October.

title: Shohei Ohtani Expected to Return Before Dodgers Regular Season Ends
author: Nelson Espinal
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani may play again this season, according to baseball operations president Andrew Friedman.
While taking a ton of champagne and celebrating a 13th National League title in 14 years, Friedman took a question about Ohtani and his outlook.
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said. “He’s progressing well. I expect him back in the regular season.”
Ohtani was not with the team in Cincinnati to celebrate the NL West title; instead, he was in Los Angeles continuing his rehabilitation on his injured right bicep and his left knee.
According to manager Dave Roberts, Ohtani had a day off on Wednesday, though he did hit off a tee and will do some hitting from a coach’s pitches at some point this week.
“There’s no pain. He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when [the] time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Does Ohtani need to play in the regular season?
The Dodgers will play Ohtani in the postseason, regardless of whether he plays in the regular season again, general manager Brandon Gomes said, focusing on how he feels rather than his season participation.
“The most important thing is that he’s healthy and in good shape. Whether it’s during the regular season or after that, as long as he’s fully prepared and ready to go, we’re fine with it,” Gomes said, per Japanese reporter Masaya Kotani.
Ohtani has mentioned in the past that he doesn’t get better from playing; rather, rest is the best medicine.
If that is the case and Ohtani can sharpen up a bit with batting practice, sitting him may ensure the Dodgers see the best version of their best player.
Ideally, fans get to see him take some swings over the next week and look better than he did before landing on the injured list.
In his last plate appearances, Ohtani struggled to rotate his body into swings and generate full extension.
He looked to wince after swings, suffering from visible pain in his right arm.
If he can swing fully and tune up his vision for the postseason, it is worth rolling him out, but the Dodgers will err on the side of caution no matter what.

title: Dodgers Manager Doesn't Know if Blake Snell Will Pitch Again in Regular Season Amid Injury
author: Gabe Smallson; Unknown
body:
Los Angeles Dodgers left-handed pitcher Blake Snell left his Wednesday start after just one inning due to a groin injury he felt pregame.
With just nine games to go in the regular season, including a crucial series against the San Diego Padres in which Snell is scheduled to start, the Dodgers are going to need the best out of their rotation moving forward.
When it comes to Snell making that potential start, the left-hander expressed confidence he'd be able to. Manager Dave Roberts, however, was noncommittal.
“It’s a possibility,” Roberts said. “I like where his head is at, but he just can’t afford any more setbacks. So, whether it’s his next start or being pushed back or whatever it is, we’ve got to make sure that he comes out ready to go in the postseason.”
Despite feeling the groin injury before trotting to the mound to start the game, Snell still wanted to push through. However, after the first inning, he decided it was better to shut things down.
“I wasn’t trying to use my lower half. It was only a couple pitches where I got into my legs and threw the ball hard,” Snell said. “Outside of that, I was kind of guiding it in there.”
Snell has had a complicated history with his groin, including ending his 2021 season about a month early, missing a few weeks in 2022 and being sidelined for two months total over the course of the 2024 campaign.
Roberts was thankful that the southpaw didn't push further through his injury.
“Obviously happy that he alerted us early to get him out of the game, not make it worse,” Roberts said. “He told me that he felt some tightness in his left groin, and it didn’t loosen up. So obviously, the right decision was to get him out. I think, No. 1 is we’ll see how he comes in tomorrow, how he feels, get some more treatment and then when we get back to L.A., then we can make that decision if we want to get imaging."
Snell himself wants to make his next start, but only time will tell if he follows through or is watching from the dugout.
“The next couple days are really going to decide,” Snell said. “But I’d love to throw on my next [scheduled start day]. Either there or a couple days after. But definitely, I want to try to get one more in the regular season.”

He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

“Obviously happy that he alerted us early to get him out of the game, not make it worse,” Roberts said. “He told me that he felt some tightness in his left groin, and it didn’t loosen up. So obviously, the right decision was to get him out. I think, No. 1 is we’ll see how he comes in tomorrow, how he feels, get some more treatment and then when we get back to L.A., then we can make that decision if we want to get imaging."
Snell himself wants to make his next start, but only time will tell if he follows through or is watching from the dugout.
“The next couple days are really going to decide,” Snell said. “But I’d love to throw on my next [scheduled start day]. Either there or a couple days after. But definitely, I want to try to get one more in the regular season.”

body:
Welcome to Waiver Wire Watch, our weekly fantasy baseball waiver wire guide. We’ll be doing things a little differently this season, with James Schiano publishing the initial waiver-wire article on Friday afternoon. Then Eric Samulski updates it every Sunday to make sure you get the most up-to-date information.
We’re doing things a little bit differently this time of year though. Rather than give a long list of players with deep analysis, there will only be a few dense player profiles for those we think currently need a bit more light shed on them. Otherwise, there will be long lists of players who can help your teams in a specific category or for this particular week.
The premise of the article is pretty straightforward. We’ll give you some recommended adds each week based on recent production or role changes. When we list a player, we’ll list the category where we think he’ll be helpful or the quick reason he’s listed. We hope this helps you determine whether the player fits your team’s needs. Not every “trending” player will be a good addition to your specific roster.
To qualify for this list, a player needs to be UNDER 40% rostered in Yahoo! formats. We understand you may say, “These players aren’t available in my league,” and we can’t help you there. These players are available in over 60% of leagues and some in 98% of leagues, so they’re available in many places, and that can hopefully satisfy readers who play in all league types.
⚾️Baseball is back on NBC: MLB returns to NBC and Peacock in 2026! In addition to becoming the exclusive home of Sunday Night Baseball, NBC Sports will broadcast MLB Sunday Leadoff, “Opening Day” and Labor Day primetime games, the first round of the MLB Draft, the entire Wild Card round of the postseason, and much more.
Fantasy Baseball Waiver Wire Hitters
Jakob Marsee - OF, MIA (49% rostered)
(BATTING AVERAGE, OBP, COUNTING STATS PLAY)
Don’t let a dreadful start to the season distract you from how productive Marsee has been lately. Across nearly 200 plate appearances since the All-Star break, he’s slashing .287/.394/.482 with six home runs, 31 runs scored, and four stolen bases. Those four steals are a tad disappointing considering how often he ran last year and how often he’s gotten on base, but he’s a great source of hits and walks right now.
Victor Mesa Jr. - OF, TBR (26% rostered)
(POWER, SPEED, PLAYING TIME)
Mesa Jr. was activated off the injured list on September 1st after missing about two weeks with a hamstring strain and has gone right back to mashing. In 12 games since, he’s hitting .383 with three homers, 12 runs scored, eight RBI, and three stolen bases. He’s also sat three times, once against a right-handed pitcher (after playing consecutive days just off the IL) and twice against lefties. He’s also started against three lefties since, so he’s in a less stringent platoon than he was back in July and August. He’s been productive across the board whenever he’s played and could be reasonably relied upon in shallower leagues this week now with closer to a full-time role.
Josue De Paula - OF, LAD (12% rostered)
(HUGE PROSPECT PROMOTION, REAL POWER)
De Paula has held his own in one week of big league action with an .789 OPS across a measly 25 plate appearance sample entering play on Friday. That’s come in six starts – one of which against a left-handed pitcher – and he hit lead-off on Tuesday against a righty. He also sat in another game against a left-handed pitcher. In that small sample, we can see that he has plus bat speed to match his elite power pedigree. Also, he’s rarely chasing pitches out of the strike zone and making contact with the ones in it. He’s attempted two stolen bases too, but been caught once. This is all very encouraging after the 21-year-old left-handed slugger jumped straight from Double-A to the big leagues and may have the best offensive profile of any prospect in the minors. In 124 games this year with Tulsa, he hit 27 home runs and stole 31 bases with a .303/.401/.547 slash line. He also rarely struck out, took his walks, and can pull the ball in the air better than most other young players. Again, De Paula is as complete a hitter that we’ve seen called up to the majors recently.
Christian Encarnacion-Strand - 1B/3B, BAL (10% rostered)
(POWER, POST HYPE BREAKOUT?)
Encarnacion-Strand has enjoyed a late season renaissance since joining the Orioles. In 51 games, he has 10 home runs, 12 doubles, and an .846 OPS. That’s come with excellent power metrics like a 15.3% barrel rate and 73.6 mph bat speed. His hit tool and overall swing decisions remain concerning, but he’s a very legitimate power threat right now while he’s consistently putting his bat on the ball.
Leo Bernal - C, STL (3% rostered)
(PROSPECT PROMOTION, HOT STREAK)
The Cardinals promoted Bernal on September 1st when the rosters expanded and he’s started all 15 games since going 18-for-61 with three home runs, three doubles, and 15 RBI. He’s started 13 games at catcher, four at designated hitter, and one at first base over that span, so it’s clear the Cardinals are doing everything they can to get his bat in the lineup everyday. A switch-hitter with real power from each side of the plate, Bernal had 16 home runs, nine stolen bases, and a 115 wRC+ through 101 games at Triple-A this season as a 22-year-old with a strong underlying profile to match. He’s a great play in deep mixed or two-catcher leagues at the moment.
Emmanual Rodríguez - OF, MIN (2% rostered)
(PROSPECT CALL-UP, POSSIBLE POWER UPSIDE)
Rodríguez put together a solid first week in the big leagues going 5-for-23 with a home run, double, and triple. That’s come with a very high average bat speed at 77.1 mph – the same as Kyle Schwarber – but has struck out in one third of his plate appearances so far. He’s started all six games too and jumped up as high as fifth in the Twins’ order on Thursday. Rodríguez slashed .262/.414/.500 with 11 homers, 33 RBI, 36 runs scored, and seven steals across 220 Triple-A plate appearances this year, and, much like Walker Jenkins, could have been called up sooner had it not been for injuries. He rarely chases pitches out of the zone and makes plenty of hard contact, which is a combination we like. Considering he’s likely going to play a bunch and has real power, he could offer a spark this week.

Fantasy Baseball Waiver Wire Pitchers
Emmet Sheehan - SP, LAD (53% rostered)
Blake Snell was removed from his start on Wednesday after one inning with left groin tightness. So, the recently optioned Sheehan might get another chance in the Dodgers’ rotation next week. Shuttled up and down a couple times recently, Sheehan returned to the big leagues for two starts after spending most of August in Triple-A and struck out 15 batters over two starts spanning 11 2/3 innings with just one earned run. He showed a renewed confidence in his fastball and that pitch was missing bats. Again, this is more speculative as Snell’s removal from his start appeared to be at least partially precautionary, but Sheehan could start at home against the Padres next week.
Justin Wrobleski - SP/RP LAD (41% rostered)
A pitcher’s upcoming schedule can be more important than their skill this time of year and Wrobleski is scheduled to face the Rafael Devers-less Giants twice to close the season. Bailey Ober and Zebby Matthews are also streaming options against the Giants. Overall, these are not a trio of pitchers we’d be running to recommend besides for this particular matchup.
Ryan Johnson - SP/RP, LAA (22% rostered)
As the Angels have overhauled their organizational pitching structure, many of their arms have made key adjustments over the last month. Johnson is part of that group, mostly trashing his sinker starting on August 11th. Since then, he has a 2.04 ERA across 39 2/3 innings. It’s still not a great profile – he’s a sidearming righty who doesn’t miss many bats and rarely throws a pitch over 90 mph besides that sinker – but he has a strong cutter, sweeper, and splitter. He’s scheduled to close the season with outings against the Twins and Mariners as a risky streaming option with good results lately.
Andrew Alvarez - SP/RP, WSN (22% rostered)
Alvarez is coming off a gem against the Angels last Saturday with a career-high seven scoreless innings, eight strikeouts, and just one hit allowed. He also walked four batters. In that game, the Angels ran out a lineup with nine right-handed hitters against the left-handed Alvarez and he tore through them with his curveball. His best pitch, it forced 10 of his 15 total whiffs and set up his auxiliary fastball and slider to get called strikes because hitters were so keyed in on the hook. His fastball leaves plenty to be desired at 92 mph with a suboptimal shape, but his curve and slider have a uniquely symbiotic relationship. David Laurila wrote about this on FanGraphs a few months back in an interview with Alvarez. Those two pitches have practically the same velocity and spin axis while the curveball has significantly more depth making hitters struggle to decipher between the two. He’s mildly trustworthy on Saturday against the Cardinals and again against the Mets next weekend.
Jonah Tong - SP, NYM (14% rostered)
Tong turned in another solid start on Monday against the Orioles going six strong with six strikeouts, one walk, and one unearned run. He pushed up his fastball usage heavily in this outing compared to his last, jumping up from 31% to 55% as he found a little bit of extra life on it. He has a huge test against the Phillies this Sunday to try and keep the momentum going before facing the Nationals next week to close the season.
Anthony Molina - RP/SP, SFG (5% rostered)
After being ripped for seven runs by the Padres last week, Molina bounced back well with 5 2/3 scoreless innings and six strikeouts on Tuesday against the Cardinals. So, it needs to be commanded in order to be consistently effective. Otherwise, that pitch is flanked by a quality curveball that’s effective against hitters from both sides of the plate, a solid slider, and a changeup that can miss bats against lefties. He’s scheduled to face the Twins at home next week to close his season.

He’s also started against three lefties since, so he’s in a less stringent platoon than he was back in July and August. He’s been productive across the board whenever he’s played and could be reasonably relied upon in shallower leagues this week now with closer to a full-time role.
Josue De Paula - OF, LAD (12% rostered)
(HUGE PROSPECT PROMOTION, REAL POWER)
De Paula has held his own in one week of big league action with an .789 OPS across a measly 25 plate appearance sample entering play on Friday. That’s come in six starts – one of which against a left-handed pitcher – and he hit lead-off on Tuesday against a righty. He also sat in another game against a left-handed pitcher. In that small sample, we can see that he has plus bat speed to match his elite power pedigree. Also, he’s rarely chasing pitches out of the strike zone and making contact with the ones in it. He’s attempted two stolen bases too, but been caught once. This is all very encouraging after the 21-year-old left-handed slugger jumped straight from Double-A to the big leagues and may have the best offensive profile of any prospect in the minors. In 124 games this year with Tulsa, he hit 27 home runs and stole 31 bases with a .303/.401/.547 slash line. He also rarely struck out, took his walks, and can pull the ball in the air better than most other young players. Again, De Paula is as complete a hitter that we’ve seen called up to the majors recently.
Christian Encarnacion-Strand - 1B/3B, BAL (10% rostered)
(POWER, POST HYPE BREAKOUT?)
Encarnacion-Strand has enjoyed a late season renaissance since joining the Orioles. In 51 games, he has 10 home runs, 12 doubles, and an .846 OPS. That’s come with excellent power metrics like a 15.3% barrel rate and 73.6 mph bat speed. His hit tool and overall swing decisions remain concerning, but he’s a very legitimate power threat right now while he’s consistently putting his bat on the ball.
Leo Bernal - C, STL (3% rostered)
(PROSPECT PROMOTION, HOT STREAK)
The Cardinals promoted Bernal on September 1st when the rosters expanded and he’s started all 15 games since going 18-for-61 with three home runs, three doubles, and 15 RBI. He’s started 13 games at catcher, four at designated hitter, and one at first base over that span, so it’s clear the Cardinals are doing everything they can to get his bat in the lineup everyday. A switch-hitter with real power from each side of the plate, Bernal had 16 home runs, nine stolen bases, and a 115 wRC+ through 101 games at Triple-A this season as a 22-year-old with a strong underlying profile to match. He’s a great play in deep mixed or two-catcher leagues at the moment.
Emmanual Rodríguez - OF, MIN (2% rostered)
(PROSPECT CALL-UP, POSSIBLE POWER UPSIDE)
Rodríguez put together a solid first week in the big leagues going 5-for-23 with a home run, double, and triple. That’s come with a very high average bat speed at 77.1 mph – the same as Kyle Schwarber – but has struck out in one third of his plate appearances so far. He’s started all six games too and jumped up as high as fifth in the Twins’ order on Thursday. Rodríguez slashed .262/.414/.500 with 11 homers, 33 RBI, 36 runs scored, and seven steals across 220 Triple-A plate appearances this year, and, much like Walker Jenkins, could have been called up sooner had it not been for injuries. He rarely chases pitches out of the zone and makes plenty of hard contact, which is a combination we like. Considering he’s likely going to play a bunch and has real power, he could offer a spark this week.
